newsitem.title: UK: London tea auctions seen hit by Burundi sanctions.
newsitem.headline: London tea auctions seen hit by Burundi sanctions.

text.p: The London tea auctions will be significantly affected if the economic blockade on Burundi is not lifted within the next six weeks, according to industry sources.

"We have enough stocks of Burundian tea to last until around Christmas but the embargo would have to be lifted by mid-November if sales from the London auctions are to continue into January," said Robin Harrison at the London Teabrokers Association (LTA).
Burundi is the second most important source of tea for the London auctions after Kenya and the auctions are the world's second biggest market-place for Burundian tea.
Ten percent of the tea sold in London so far in 1996 came from Burundi after Kenya tea accounted for 70 percent.
"Around 300,000 packages of tea (55 kilos each) destined for export and bought before the embargo have been impounded at Dar Es Salaam," said the LTA's Harrison.
The port of Dar Es Salaam in Tanzania handles the bulk of landlocked Burundi's tea exports.
The UK is its main export market outside Africa and sources in Africa said the UK is currently the only export market able to sell, due to the sanctions.
The effect of the embargo on the price of Burundi tea is uncertain but brokers said Kenya and Rwanda are the most likely source of replacement business if stocks run out.

"It could be that stocks of impounded tea would be unsaleable after months of being stored in the heat but in the meantime, the Burundian tea growers association say that production is continuing as normal," Harrison said.
But Britain's tea drinkers will not have to suffer.
"Although the UK imports around 2,000 of the 6,000 tonnes of tea exported by Burundi, it only accounts for one to two percent of UK tea imports," said a spokesman for the Tea Council.
"But Burundi is a very popular source of high quality tea for use in blends in the UK, Irish and Pakistan markets," he added.
Tea and coffee exports are the main means of hard currency earnings for Burundi.

Burundi's neighbours, including Tanzania and Kenya, imposed sanctions on it at the end of July in protest at the military coup which installed Pierre Buyoya as president. -London Newsroom, +44 171 542 8071
